Incontinent
in-KON-ti-nent
adjective
From the Latin in- (“not”) + continens, “holding together, restraining oneself” (from continere, “to hold in”); hence without self-restraint, unable to hold oneself in. The modern narrowing to a bodily infirmity has all but hidden the moral sense the KJV intends.

Biblical Definition

Incontinent in the KJV is a word of the will, not of the body. It means without self-control, unrestrained, unable to hold oneself in — the man who has no rule over his appetites and passions. The modern ear hears only the bodily infirmity the word has since come to name, but Paul means a moral ruin. Cataloguing the marks of the last days, he lists the men from whom the godly must turn away: “without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good” (2Ti 3:3). The incontinent man stands in that grim company because his sin is the same root as theirs — a self given wholly over to itself, ungoverned, spilling out in every direction. The wise man had drawn his picture long before: “He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls” (Pro 25:28) — defenceless, open to every enemy, because the inner restraint is gone. Against this stands the fruit of the Spirit, whose last-named grace is the very opposite: “temperance” — self-control — “against such there is no law” (Gal 5:23). And the runner in the games is Paul’s living emblem of it: “every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things” (1Co 9:25), disciplining body and desire to win a corruptible crown, that we might win an incorruptible. Continence is not native to fallen man; it is the Spirit’s gift and the saint’s daily discipline.

Webster 1828 Definition

Without self-restraint; unable to govern one’s appetites and passions — a moral fault, not the modern bodily sense.

INCONTINENT, unrestrained; not governing the appetites; lacking self-control.

From Latin in- (“not”) + continens, “holding oneself in.”

The KJV means a moral want of restraint, not the later bodily sense.

Paul lists the incontinent among the marks of the last days (2Ti 3:3).

Its opposite is temperance, the fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:23).

Key Scripture

2Ti 3:3 — "Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good,"

Pro 25:28 — "He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls."

Gal 5:23 — "Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law."

1Co 9:25 — "And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible."

Modern Corruption

A moral word narrowed to a bodily one; it recovers self-control as the Spirit’s fruit and the mark that parts the disciplined saint from the ungoverned world.

expand to see more

The drift here has hidden a moral word behind a medical one. To modern ears “incontinent” names a bodily infirmity and nothing more; a man is not blamed for it, and rightly so where it is mere weakness of the flesh. But Paul’s word is not of the body but of the will. His incontinent man is the man without self-command — ungoverned in appetite, temper, and tongue — and he is named among trucebreakers and false accusers, not among the sick. To read the modern sense into 2Ti 3:3 is to turn a charge of sin into a note of misfortune, and to miss that the apostle is describing a generation in love with its own unrestraint.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that self-control is a Christian grace, not a natural gift. Fallen man is by nature a city broken down and without walls, his passions loose and his spirit unruled; and an age that bids every man follow his desires and never deny himself only tears the last stones from the wall. Scripture says the opposite. Temperance is the fruit of the Spirit; the runner in the games is temperate in all things; and he that ruleth his own spirit is stronger than he that taketh a city. Continence is won, not inherited — wrought in the believer by the Spirit and pursued by daily discipline. The incontinent life is not freedom but a ruin open to every enemy; the governed life, under God, is the only liberty.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means without self-restraint, ungoverned in appetite and passion — a moral fault, not the modern bodily one.

Incontinent — Latin in- (“not”) + continens, “holding in.”

It means without self-control, unable to hold oneself in.

The KJV sense is moral; the modern bodily sense is a later narrowing.

Paul lists the incontinent among the perilous men of the last days (2Ti 3:3).

Usage

"Incontinent means without self-control: Paul names it among the sins of the last days."

"The incontinent man “hath no rule over his own spirit” — a city broken down and without walls."

"Against the incontinent stands the runner, temperate in all things for an incorruptible crown."
